Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I am permanently an outsider now
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Chloe first noticed how her mind had fractured into a hundred disconnected shards the afternoon she rode the number 42 bus home. She had been mentally rehearsing monologues when a man in the back row suddenly stood, drew a long pistol, and fired twice before a uniformed officer tackled him. Her brain refused to compile the incident into a coherent story, leaving only nonverbal sensory flashes: the copper taste of panic, the jarring screech of metal, and the sight of responding police with drawn weapons. Because she could not piece the event together into a single narrative, the fragmented pieces refused to settle, leaving her body braced for an attack that had already ended. Within weeks, the sensory fragments began to surface without warning. When she remembered the frightening event, she felt like it was happening right now, her heart hammering until negative emotions like fear and horror flooded her chest. This constant physiological alarm meant her threat response never powered down, and the resulting hypervigilance pulled the disjointed memories back into her consciousness every time she passed a crowded street. The persistent sense of danger made it impossible to trust her surroundings, even when her peers insisted she was safe in a locked studio, and the relentless dread convinced her that accountability was an illusion, hardening her belief that justice would never come. As the official case was quietly closed, Chloe learned that the people responsible would face no consequences, a fact that settled into her chest like a stone. She had come to believe she was permanently an outsider now, watching life unfold behind an invisible barrier. Because she viewed the world as irredeemably dangerous and herself as fundamentally set apart, the negative appraisals directly amplified her threat monitoring, keeping her in a state of chronic hypervigilance. Her outsider identity also made the memory fragments lose their temporal boundaries, transforming disjointed pieces into relentless intrusions, while the deep conviction that she was cut off from normal life directly fed into her maladaptive strategies, pushing her toward rigid avoidance and impulsive shopping. To stop the panic from spiking, Chloe began avoiding military or police uniforms and weapons wherever they appeared in her daily life. She stopped taking public transport altogether, switching to expensive rideshares that drained her savings. Driven by an urgent need to quiet the noise, she spent money impulsively to distract or comfort herself, purchasing costume pieces and luxury items she never used. The isolation she felt as an outsider deepened with every avoided route and every empty shopping bag, the maladaptive strategies reinforcing her belief that she was permanently set apart. Because her avoidance behaviors kept her physically controlled but psychologically rigid, the threat response only intensified, making every potential danger feel imminent. Over the following year, the cycle tightened around her acting career. Each time the memories surfaced unbidden, the resulting horror reinforced her negative appraisals, convincing her that the world was irredeemably dangerous. Her compulsive spending and rigid avoidance meant she missed two major callbacks, and her director gently noted that her unavailability was harming her professional standing. She finally booked an intake appointment after a casting director asked why she flinched at a prop rifle, a moment that made her realize her avoidance was costing her everything she loved. Chloe sits in the therapist's office now, terrified that the panic will return if she stops controlling her environment, yet quietly hoping to reclaim the voice she used to love so much.
